title: Design internet and hybrid connectivity
learningObjective: Recommend connectivity between Azure resources and the internet (inbound and outbound) and between Azure and on-premises networks.
foundation: Connectivity design answers three questions: how do users reach the app, how does the app reach the internet, and how does Azure reach the office?
Inbound web traffic goes through a protected front door. Outbound traffic should leave through a known exit. Offices connect over a VPN or a private ExpressRoute line.
engineer: Internet inbound: Azure Front Door (global HTTP(S), WAF, caching), Application Gateway (regional HTTP(S), WAF), public Standard Load Balancer for non-HTTP, all with DDoS Protection on public IPs; Azure Firewall DNAT for controlled inbound to private services. Outbound: new VNets use private subnets (no default outbound access), so give explicit outbound with NAT gateway (static IPs, scalable SNAT), Azure Firewall (filtered egress in a hub) or load balancer outbound rules.

Hybrid: site-to-site VPN (IPsec over the internet, VPN gateway active-active and zone-redundant SKUs, BGP), point-to-site VPN for users, ExpressRoute (private connection through a provider; private peering to VNets and Microsoft peering to Microsoft 365/PaaS public endpoints; Global Reach to connect sites through Microsoft's backbone; FastPath to bypass the gateway for performance; ExpressRoute Direct for 10/100 Gbps ports), ExpressRoute with site-to-site VPN as failover, and Azure Virtual WAN for large global hub-and-spoke designs with branches, VPN, ExpressRoute and secured hubs.

Topology: hub-and-spoke with shared services (gateways, firewall, Bastion, DNS) in the hub and gateway transit to spokes, or Virtual WAN managed hubs; Azure Virtual Network Manager to manage connectivity and security admin rules at scale.

example.title: Connecting a manufacturer
body: Head office and two factories connect to the Azure hub with ExpressRoute; a site-to-site VPN is the backup path. Forty small sales offices join through Virtual WAN with SD-WAN partners.

Public web apps sit behind Front Door with WAF. Spoke subnets reach the internet only through Azure Firewall in the hub, and batch VMs that call a partner API use a NAT gateway with two static IPs the partner allow-lists.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription; most design reviews need only Reader access
permissions: Reader to review existing resources; Contributor or Owner to build the design
limits: Check service limits and regional availability for each component
portal: Virtual network gateway: VPN or ExpressRoute, SKU, active-active, zone-redundant.
ExpressRoute circuit: provider, bandwidth, peering; connection to the gateway.
NAT gateway: public IPs, associate with subnets.
Virtual WAN: hubs, VPN/ExpressRoute gateways, secured hub.
configuration.cli:
az network nat gateway create -g rg-net -n natgw-batch --public-ip-addresses pip-nat1 pip-nat2 --idle-timeout 10
az network vnet subnet update -g rg-net --vnet-name vnet-spoke -n batch --nat-gateway natgw-batch
az network vnet-gateway create -g rg-net -n vpngw-hub --vnet vnet-hub --gateway-type Vpn --sku VpnGw2AZ --public-ip-addresses pip-vpn1

expected: NAT gateway for predictable outbound; ExpressRoute for private, predictable hybrid
failureScenarios: Using only VPN when the requirement says 'not over the internet'
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: VMs in a new VNet can't reach the internet.
troubleshooting.cause: Private subnets have no default outbound access.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a NAT gateway, firewall route or public IP.

troubleshooting.symptom: Partner rejects calls because the source IP keeps changing.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a NAT gateway with static public IPs.

comparisons.difference: VPN: encrypted over the internet, quick and cheap; ExpressRoute: private, predictable, higher bandwidth and cost.
Self-managed hub VNets vs Microsoft-managed hubs with built-in any-to-any routing at scale.

misconceptions.myth: ExpressRoute traffic is encrypted by default.
misconceptions.reality: It is private but not encrypted; add MACsec (Direct) or IPsec over ExpressRoute if required.
New VNets use private subnets by default.

architectureDecisions: Front Door/App Gateway + WAF for inbound web.
Explicit outbound: NAT gateway or firewall.
ExpressRoute (with VPN backup) for critical hybrid; Virtual WAN for many sites.

walkthrough.subtitle: Let users in safely, let apps out predictably, and connect offices privately.

steps.label: Problem
steps.title: Three directions of traffic
body: Customers come in from the internet, apps call partner APIs, and offices need private access to Azure.

steps.label: Inbound
steps.title: A protected front door
body: Front Door (global) or Application Gateway (regional) receives web traffic with a web application firewall. Non-web traffic uses a public load balancer. DDoS Protection guards public IPs.

steps.label: Outbound
steps.title: A known exit
body: New subnets have no automatic internet access. A NAT gateway gives a subnet fixed public IPs for outbound calls; or route traffic through Azure Firewall in the hub to filter it.

steps.label: Hybrid
steps.title: VPN, ExpressRoute, Virtual WAN
body: VPN: encrypted tunnel over the internet, quick to set up. ExpressRoute: private line through a provider, predictable and fast; keep a VPN as backup. Virtual WAN: Microsoft-managed hubs for many branches and regions.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Connectivity design
recap: Front Door / App Gateway + WAF; DDoS Protection
NAT gateway or firewall for outbound
VPN, ExpressRoute (+ VPN backup), Virtual WAN
